children: Cost of funds is emerging as a key differentiator for Indian banks, influencing margins, credit costs, loan growth and investor valuations

The cost of raising deposits and other liabilities is emerging as a critical dividing line between Indian banks, with funding efficiency increasingly influencing net interest margins, credit costs, growth and investor valuations, according to an ICICI Securities sector report released on September 22 .

The report said a competitive cost of funds (CoF) gives lenders greater room to maintain margins and expand their loan books without moving up the risk curve. Historically, CASA deposits have been an important indicator of this advantage, although the funding mix also depends on savings-account pricing, term deposits, borrowings and net worth.
Lower Funding Costs Support Margins, Asset Quality

The report argued that the importance of CoF has increased as lending becomes more competitive and a large portion of bank loans remains linked to external benchmark rates. In such an environment, lenders have limited ability to pass higher funding costs through loan pricing, putting pressure on NIMs.

ICICI Securities also identified a strong correlation between CoF and medium-term credit costs. A higher funding cost can push lenders towards riskier lending strategies to generate comparable returns, while a lower CoF can support similar returns without requiring a higher risk appetite.

The report noted that changes in relative CoF positions have historically coincided with changes in bank valuations. It cited Kotak Mahindra Bank’s improved CoF competitiveness during FY17-19 as one factor behind its re-rating, while the deterioration in HDFC Bank’s CoF position after its merger was cited as one factor behind its subsequent de-rating.
HDFC Bank Faces CASA, Funding Cost Gap

HDFC Bank has improved its funding profile since the merger, with its borrowing share declining to 13 per cent from a post-merger peak of 25 per cent, according to the report. However, its CASA share remains about 600 basis points below Axis Bank’s, contributing to a funding-cost disadvantage.

The report also highlighted Federal Bank, RBL Bank, Karur Vysya Bank, Indian Bank and Bank of Maharashtra for different combinations of funding-cost performance and growth. Federal Bank’s recent re-rating was partly attributed to improved CoF and CASA execution, while RBL could benefit from the opportunity to strengthen its long-tenure deposit base through FCNR(B) deposits.
CASA, Deposit Mix Shape Funding Advantage

ICICI Securities said CASA generally has an inverse relationship with cost of deposits, although banks offering higher savings-account rates can be exceptions. The report’s Q1FY27 analysis also showed that banks relying more heavily on relatively expensive term deposits face greater pressure on CoF as they pursue faster growth.

For lenders, the challenge is therefore to balance deposit mobilisation with funding efficiency. Cutting deposit rates may improve CoF but can constrain scale, while aggressive deposit pricing can support growth at the expense of margins. The report said FCNR(B) deposits could provide an opportunity for Kotak Mahindra Bank and RBL Bank to increase their share of longer-tenure deposits competitively.
